extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American press history / journalism scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards about producing and understanding newspapers in the United States c.1783–1801, especially the partisan (party) press — its purposes, formats, economics, and rhetorical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of timely commercial news for merchants
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the mercantile classes with up-to-the-minute news of the arrival of sailing vessels and the offerings of importers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily journalism was adopted to serve merchants more efficiently than coffee-house records; include lists of 'ships entered' and cargo descriptions to attract and serve a mercantile audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing determines audience reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of six cents a copy ... put these papers beyond the reach of the popular audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set price strategically: higher price can target mercantile/class readership; lower price tends to broaden popular readership and is characteristic of political papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan alignment as expected norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of these mercantile papers had strong partisan leanings. Political independence, for man or newspaper, was virtually unknown in this era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and design newspapers as political organs or party spokesmen rather than neutrally independent publications; partisan content and overt advocacy are normal features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation between mercantile and political papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the aims of these two groups seem to be divergent, no sharp line can be drawn between them. Perhaps the distinguishing badge was price: the political papers commonly sold for less than the mercantile journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use price, content emphasis, and target audience to position a paper as mercantile (commercial news, higher price) or political (broader/popular reach, lower price).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of major political issues and debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers were immediately filled with discussions of complicated but fundamental questions (e.g., adoption of the Federal Constitution) and published influential series such as The Federalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish reprints, essays, and serialized arguments on foundational political questions; high-quality ordered, clear exposition (as in The Federalist) is a mark of influential political journalism, while some contemporaneous writing could be 'scurrilous and unworthy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the press as a vehicle for party propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: The fight [over ratification] was bitter ... Out of this contest ... came the two great parties ... Newspapers were widely partisan and used to promote party positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize editorial content to advocate party positions, mobilize supporters, and attack opponents; expect heavy use of essays, satires, and invective during campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency/format tuned to information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The wish to provide the mercantile classes with up-to-the-minute news ... the men who adapted such information to daily journalism ... served the merchants more efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose publishing frequency (daily, semiweekly, etc.) to match audience needs for timeliness — e.g., daily for fast commercial or political news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial mission and presentation (dignity vs commerce)
rubrics_metrics.description: To hold up the people’s own government, in a favorable point of light — and to impress just ideas of its administration by exhibiting FACTS ... Fenno excluded advertising— at first — as interfering with the dignity of his project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate a clear editorial mission and consider layout choices (indices, exclusion/inclusion of advertising) to uphold perceived dignity or seriousness; know there is a tradeoff between dignity and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue model: subscriptions, advertising, public printing, and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Its top circulation was 1,400, of which only 1,000 went to bona fide subscribers. Such public printing as it had received had not been sufficient to balance its losses from delinquent subscriptions. By this time it had been driven to solicit advertising ... Fenno appealed to Hamilton ... for a loan of $2,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan multiple revenue streams (subscriptions, advertising, government/public printing contracts, wealthy patrons/loans). Collection of subscription accounts and advertising are decisive for survival; lack of patronage can cause failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and subscription health as success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Top circulation was 1,400, of which only 1,000 went to bona fide subscribers ... had difficulty collecting subscription accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report bona fide subscribers separately from total circulation; sustainability depends on real subscriber payments, not just numbers printed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of prominent contributors to enhance authority
rubrics_metrics.description: His paper, with its contributions from Hamilton, Adams, and other leading Federalists, kept to a fairly high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit contributions from recognized political leaders and experts to increase credibility and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire, lampoon, and verse as political tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Freneau’s favorite method was satire, in parable, versified lampoon, and hyperbole; ... His paper widened the breach ... his paper ... had more than a little to do with the ultimate dissolution of the Federalist party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire and literary forms as powerful rhetorical tools to attack opponents and mobilize sentiment, but be aware these methods can provoke strong backlash and legal/physical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest and ethics concerns when tied to government
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton ... inserted an anonymous letter ... questioning the ethics of 'vilifying' an administration from which the editor received a salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose or avoid relationships (salaries, positions) that could be construed as compromising editorial independence; expect accusations of being a 'personal organ' if ties exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as public censor — normative role
rubrics_metrics.description: No government ought to be without censors: and where the press is free, no one ever will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the normative role of the press to criticize and check government actions as part of civic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and physical risks: libel suits, violence, and office attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Federalist rowdies wrecked the Aurora printing office and beat the editor ... Porcupine's Gazette ... crowning misfortune was a $5,000 verdict against it for libeling Philadelphia’s most famous physician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate legal exposure (libel suits) and physical danger in highly partisan climates; balance aggressive rhetoric against potential legal and personal costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/national scope and following the seat of government
rubrics_metrics.description: When the seat of government was removed to Philadelphia in 1791, the Gazette followed ... Fenno aimed at national circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide geographic scope (local, regional, national); proximity to political centers can affect access to contributors, sponsorship, and national influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content variety to engage readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical poems and parables, as well as essays in sober earnest, were devoted to [issues] ... newspaper argument and propaganda did not end with choice of electors, but pressure was exerted ... papers overran with electioneering essays, squibs, and invectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix literary forms (poems, parables), essays, letters, and polemic to attract readers and convey political messages; variety increases engagement but may vary in seriousness and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution control (post office, circulation channels) shapes reach
rubrics_metrics.description: It was widely charged ... that the Federalists had used their control of the postoffice to prevent the circulation of Antifederalist papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and manage distribution channels and postal access; political control of distribution can limit or extend a paper's influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial fragility of political organs
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the National Gazette came suddenly ... Jefferson ... had retired ... yellow fever epidemic ... Freneau and his printers were virtually bankrupt. The business of publishing political organs did not pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for contingencies (epidemics, loss of patronage) and be realistic about the financial sustainability of highly partisan publications; political influence does not guarantee profitability.
